label: Sequences, series and power series — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The interval of convergence of the power series Σ(n = 0 to ∞) |x − 5|ⁿ / ((n + 1)(n + 2)) is:
options: unbounded — it converges for all x
items.explanation: Put t = |x − 5|. Then |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = (n+3)/(n+1) → 1, so the radius is 1 about the centre 5, giving 4 < x < 6. This is June 2026 Q28; the marked option claimed an infinite radius, which would need factorial coefficients. Note that the series in fact also converges AT 4 and 6, since Σ1/((n+1)(n+2)) telescopes to 1 — but (4, 6) is the only option with the correct centre and radius.

items.stem: The radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n! is:
items.explanation: aₙ = 1/n!, so |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = (n+1)!/n! = n + 1 → ∞. The factorial defeats any power of x, so the series converges for every real x — it is eˣ. Checked: forty terms at x = 1 give 2.7182818284590455 against e = 2.718281828459045.

items.stem: The radius of convergence of Σ n! xⁿ is:
items.explanation: Now the factorial is in the numerator: |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = n!/(n+1)! = 1/(n+1) → 0. The series converges only at x = 0, where every term beyond the first vanishes. It is the exact mirror of Σxⁿ/n!.

items.stem: Σ 1/nᵖ converges if and only if:
items.explanation: Strict inequality. At p = 1 this is the harmonic series, which diverges despite its terms tending to zero, so p ≥ 1 is wrong; and p = 1/2 diverges, so p > 0 is wrong. At p = 2 the sum is π²/6 ≈ 1.6449.

items.stem: The harmonic series Σ 1/n:
items.explanation: It diverges, slowly. π²/6 is the sum of Σ1/n², and log 2 is the sum of the ALTERNATING harmonic series Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n — both are different series and both are standard distractors here.

items.stem: Absolute convergence implies:
items.explanation: If Σ|aₙ| converges then Σaₙ converges. The converse fails: Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n converges while Σ1/n does not, which is what 'conditionally convergent' names. Inside its radius a power series always converges absolutely.

items.stem: The interval of convergence of Σ(n = 1 to ∞) (x − 2)ⁿ/n is:
items.explanation: The radius is 1 about the centre 2, giving the open interval (1, 3). At x = 1 the series is Σ(−1)ⁿ/n, which converges by the alternating series test; at x = 3 it is Σ1/n, the harmonic series, which diverges. So the left endpoint is in and the right is out: [1, 3). Stopping at the radius gives option B and loses the mark.

items.stem: The interval of convergence of Σ (x + 3)ⁿ/2ⁿ is:
items.explanation: The series is Σ((x+3)/2)ⁿ, geometric in (x+3)/2, so it converges exactly when |x + 3| < 2, giving −5 < x < −1. At both endpoints the ratio has modulus 1 and the terms are ±1, which fails the nᵗʰ-term test, so both ends diverge and the interval is open.

items.stem: Σ(n = 1 to ∞) 1/(n(n + 1)) equals:
items.explanation: By partial fractions 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1), so the partial sum to N is 1 − 1/(N+1), which tends to 1. Option C is Σ1/n², a different series. Summed numerically to 0.9999995 over two million terms.
items.check: The telescoping leaves only the first term, so the answer is the first term of the first bracket — here 1/1.

items.stem: For Σ aₙxⁿ with aₙ = 3ⁿ, the radius of convergence is:
items.explanation: |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = 3ⁿ/3ⁿ⁺¹ = 1/3. The root test agrees in one step: |aₙ|^(1/n) = 3, so 1/R = 3. The series is geometric in 3x and converges exactly when |3x| < 1. Option B inverts the ratio, which is the standard slip.
items.check: Growing coefficients must give a SMALL radius, so an answer above 1 is wrong by inspection.

items.stem: The series Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n is:
items.explanation: It converges by the alternating series test, to ln 2 = 0.693147, but the series of absolute values Σ1/n diverges — so it is convergent without being absolutely convergent, which is the definition of conditional convergence.

items.stem: Consider the tests for convergence of a series.
items.explanation: A is the nᵗʰ-term test, valid in that one direction. B is true, with the alternating harmonic series as witness. C is true and is why endpoints need separate work. D is false — terms tending to zero proves nothing, as the harmonic series shows.
statements: If the terms of a convergent series are aₙ, then aₙ → 0.
A convergent series need not be absolutely convergent.
At |x − c| = R the ratio test is inconclusive.

A.why: True. Convergence forces the terms to vanish, which is why a series whose terms do not tend to zero diverges immediately — the quickest way to dispose of a geometric endpoint.

B.why: True. Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n converges to ln 2 while Σ1/n diverges, so the series is conditionally but not absolutely convergent.

C.why: True, and it is the definition of the radius rather than a defect: the ratio limit equals exactly 1 there, so the test returns no verdict and a different test must be used.

D.why: False, and it is the most expensive error in the topic. The harmonic series has terms tending to zero and still diverges. The nᵗʰ-term test runs one way only.

items.stem: Why does every power series whose coefficients are a ratio of polynomials in n have radius 1?
options: because |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| is then a ratio of equal-degree polynomials, which tends to 1
because the terms tend to zero
because the series is then geometric
items.explanation: Replacing n by n + 1 does not change the degree, so |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| is a ratio of polynomials of equal degree and tends to the ratio of leading coefficients, namely 1. June 2026's coefficients 1/((n+1)(n+2)) give (n+3)/(n+1) → 1. The practical consequence is that for such series all the work is at the endpoints.

items.stem: At the endpoints of June 2026's series, x = 4 and x = 6, the series becomes Σ1/((n+1)(n+2)), whose sum is:
items.explanation: Partial fractions give 1/(n+1) − 1/(n+2), so the partial sums telescope to 1 − 1/(N+2) → 1. The series therefore CONVERGES at both endpoints, so its true convergence set is the closed interval [4, 6], even though the exam's options give the open one.
items.check: Summed numerically to 0.9999995 over two million terms. The coefficients behave like 1/n², and a p-series with p = 2 converges.

items.stem: Which of these series has radius of convergence 0?
items.explanation: A factorial in the NUMERATOR makes |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = 1/(n+1) → 0, so the series converges only at x = 0. Option B has the factorial in the denominator and radius ∞; options A and D have rational coefficients and radius 1.

items.stem: A power series has radius of convergence 2 about the centre 1. Its interval of convergence:
options: contains (−1, 3) and may or may not contain the endpoints
items.explanation: The radius settles the open interval and nothing more; whether −1 and 3 belong depends on the series obtained by substituting them, and all three bracket patterns are possible. This lesson contains one example of each: [4, 6], [1, 3) and (−5, −1).

items.stem: Consider the three series Σ|x−5|ⁿ/((n+1)(n+2)), Σ(x−2)ⁿ/n and Σ(x+3)ⁿ/2ⁿ.
items.explanation: A is true: the first two both have radius 1. B is true, by telescoping. C is true: the terms are ±1 at each end. D is false — the first series converges at both endpoints, so its convergence set is closed, not half-open.
statements: The first two series both have radius of convergence 1.
The first series converges at both of its endpoints, because Σ1/((n+1)(n+2)) = 1.
The third series diverges at both endpoints by the nᵗʰ-term test.
The first series has a half-open interval of convergence.

A.why: True. Both have rational coefficients, so |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| is a ratio of equal-degree polynomials tending to 1.

B.why: True. Partial fractions give 1/(n+1) − 1/(n+2) and the partial sums telescope to 1 − 1/(N+2) → 1, so the convergence set is the closed interval [4, 6].

C.why: True. At x = −5 and x = −1 the ratio (x+3)/2 has modulus 1, so the terms are ±1 and do not tend to zero — divergence follows immediately.

D.why: False. Both endpoints converge, so the interval is CLOSED, [4, 6]. The half-open case in this lesson is Σ(x−2)ⁿ/n on [1, 3), where the two endpoints behave differently.

items.stem: Why can the two endpoints of a single power series behave differently?
options: they cannot — both endpoints always behave the same way
because the radius is measured differently on each side
because the ratio test gives different limits at each end
at the boundary the absolute series is on the knife edge, so convergence depends on the sign pattern, and the two endpoints differ precisely in their signs
items.explanation: Inside the radius the terms are dominated by a convergent geometric series, so convergence is absolute and signs are irrelevant. At |x − c| = R that domination is lost and the absolute series sits exactly on the boundary, so only cancellation can rescue it. Substituting x = c − R gives alternating signs and x = c + R gives constant ones, which is why Σ(x−2)ⁿ/n converges at 1 and diverges at 3.

items.stem: Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n equals:
items.explanation: The alternating series test gives convergence, and the value follows from the expansion ln(1 + x) = Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹xⁿ/n, valid for |x| < 1, extended to x = 1 by Abel's theorem — which applies precisely because the series converges there. Option B is Σ1/n².
items.check: Summed numerically over two million terms: 0.693147, matching ln 2 = 0.693147 to six decimals.

items.stem: An analyst evaluates 1/(1 − x) at x = 1.5 using 1 + x + x² + ⋯ and reports a truncated partial sum. The best description is:
options: the series converges slowly, so more terms are needed
the identity holds only for |x| < 1, so the partial sums diverge and more terms make the estimate worse
the answer is correct but the sign must be reversed
the series converges to −2 but very slowly
items.explanation: The terms 1.5ⁿ grow without bound, so the nᵗʰ-term test already forces divergence; the partial sums 1, 2.5, 4.75, 8.125, … climb away from the true value −2. Outside the radius the identity is simply false, and truncating gives no approximation at all — which is why the radius must be checked before a series is used, not after the answer looks wrong.
